Senses.PreferredTarget: a hero in chaotic times
AlternateTargets: a hero of troubled times
Senses.Explanation: “A hero in chaotic times” characterizes drastic, forceful action as suited to disorder, usually in a pointed contrast with “a traitor in peaceful times.” Baichi Xingyuan and Yuan'an Liao apply the pair to blows and shouts versus refined talk. Baiyu Jingsi applies the hero half critically to Nanquan's killing of the cat. Lianfeng Su uses it for Yunmen's violent response to the newborn Buddha. Huiyue Xu turns the contrast into a warning at Bodhidharma's memorial.
Senses.Note: The expression is often ironic or double-edged, not simple praise. Its force comes from judging conduct against its conditions: what looks heroic amid disorder may itself be violent or out of place.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Yuanwu Keqin explains Xuedou's verse on Yunmen's bowl of rice and bucket of water. He rejects searching for a subtle theory underneath the plain answer, then warns that trying to understand without understanding and trying to stop without stopping only spills out a muddle-bag. He connects this hesitation with the verse's sons without trousers and quotes Hanshan afterward. Yuanwu voices the diagnosis to his audience; Yunmen and Xuedou supply the inherited material under examination.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1382.xml). In written instruction to monk Yue, Wuzhun Shifan compares learning with the moon waxing and then losing its light, beyond anything one can display to another. He recalls Guling returning to his teacher and claiming to be as he was before traveling. Yue now plans to visit his living teacher and father, so Wuzhun warns him first not to imitate Guling by spilling out a muddle-bag. He fears the teacher might act like Deshan and render even this written scroll waste paper. The phrase is Wuzhun's present warning against borrowed self-presentation, addressed to Yue.

Senses.Explanation: Spilling out a muddle-bag rebukes a confused attempt to present understanding. Yuanwu applies it to hesitation over Yunmen's answer, while Wuzhun warns a departing student against making a borrowed performance before his teacher. Neither passage recommends bewilderment as a way to teach. Yuanwu Keqin explains Xuedou's verse on Yunmen's bowl of rice and bucket of water. He rejects searching for a subtle theory underneath the plain answer, then warns that trying to understand without understanding and trying to stop without stopping only spills out a muddle-bag. He connects this hesitation with the verse's sons without trousers and quotes Hanshan afterward. Yuanwu voices the diagnosis to his audience; Yunmen and Xuedou supply the inherited material under examination. In written instruction to monk Yue, Wuzhun Shifan compares learning with the moon waxing and then losing its light, beyond anything one can display to another. He recalls Guling returning to his teacher and claiming to be as he was before traveling. Yue now plans to visit his living teacher and father, so Wuzhun warns him first not to imitate Guling by spilling out a muddle-bag. He fears the teacher might act like Deshan and render even this written scroll waste paper. The phrase is Wuzhun's present warning against borrowed self-presentation, addressed to Yue.

Senses.PreferredTarget: put a question
AlternateTargets: pose a question
bestow a question
Senses.Explanation: Literally, to let a question descend or to bestow a question. In Chan records it marks the bestowing master putting a question to monks and requiring an answer. The heading “questions put in the room” places it in the entering-interview setting; one such question asks how the patriarchal mind-seal is inscribed and how deep the buddhas' source is. An unnamed monk later recalls a question bestowed the previous day—“since it is not mind, not buddha, and not a thing, what is it after all?”—and returns to request instruction. Records also show questions put before a group: on a snowy day Pin Jixiang asks why the solitary peak is not white when snow covers the thousand mountains, and elsewhere monks give several replies to “when there is no buddha in the hall, what then?”, none of which Guxue Zhe accepts. The term therefore names an observable part of Chan's interview machinery: the bestowing master publicly or privately puts the question, monks answer or fail to answer, and the record preserves the ensuing acceptance, rejection, substitute response, shout, or blow.
Senses.Note: The literal downward/bestowing graph is retained in the alternate target, but ordinary English “put a question” best fits the repeated record headings and speaker turns. It is related to asking (問), public question-and-answer, answers supplied for others, and entering the room, but is not interchangeable with them.

Senses.Explanation: An indication is an address or showing offered to an assembly or interlocutor. The same referent appears as an act, a fixed case-preface rubric, and a catalogued textual item; these are grammatical and editorial packages, not different things. The compound occurs 721 times in 201 source files. The Blue Cliff Record's fixed rubric “the indication says” (垂示云) introduces Yuanwu Keqin's pointer before a case. One begins, “a phrase that settles heaven and earth, honored through ten thousand generations” (定乾坤句。萬世共遵。). Yunmen Wenyan's Extended Record counts “185 items of essential chamber sayings; 290 items of indications and substitute answers” (室中語要一百八十五則垂示代語二百九十則). Tianyin Yuanxiu's record prints “chamber indication” (室中垂示) before his words. Public interviews expose the same act from the requesting side: unnamed monks ask Jiufeng Qin and Shoushan Xingnian to offer an indication, while Touzi Datong asks Cuiwei Wuxue. The answers—including Cuiwei's ‘Do you want a second ladle of foul water?’—show Zen bending ordinary indication into a named teaching-seat event that can be requested, delivered, prefaced, and collected.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Like someone climbing a mountain, each must make their own effort
AlternateTargets: As when climbing a mountain, each person must strive for themselves

Senses.Note: A mountain cannot be climbed by another person on one’s behalf. Gaofeng uses the pair amid instructions for unbroken effort; Tianru follows a warning about death and delay with it. Shixi turns from an inherited case to his listeners’ responsibility, and Yuejiang uses it after describing the barriers they make of sensory experience. The image urges personal effort without claiming that teachers or companions are useless.

Occurrences.Kwic: 樞機，似一滴投於巨壑。到遮裏有甚麼禪道可參？有甚麼佛法可學？有甚麼生死可脫？有甚麼涅槃可證？騰騰任運，任運騰騰。臘月三十日到來，管取得大自在，去住自由。故云：自從認得曹溪路，了知生死不相干。然雖如是，豎拂子云：且道遮箇是生耶？是死耶？若也道得，便可向無佛處稱尊，無法處說法。其或未然，山僧不懼羞慚，更與諸人露箇消息。擲下拂子云：夜冷魚潛空下釣，不如收卷過殘年。兄弟家成，十年二十年撥草瞻風，不見佛性，往往皆謂被昏沈掉舉之所籠󰋪，殊不知只遮昏沈掉舉四字，當體即是佛性。堪嗟迷人不了，妄自執法為病，以病攻病，致使佛性愈求愈遠，轉急轉遲。設使一箇半箇回光返照，直下知非，廓然藥病兩忘，眼睛露出，洞明達磨單傳，徹見本來佛性。若據西峰點檢將來，猶是生死岸頭事；若曰向上一路，須知更在青山外。若論此事，正如逆水撑船，上得一篙，退去十篙，上得十篙，退去千篙，愈撑愈退，退之又退，直饒退到大洋海底，掇轉船頭，決欲又要向彼中撑上。若具遮般操志，即是到家消息。如人上山，各自努力。若論此事，如萬丈深潭中投一塊石相似，透頂透底，了無絲毫間隔。誠能如是用工，如是無間，一七日中若無倒斷，妙上座永墮阿鼻地獄。法門廣無邊，參禪第一義。若真師子兒，不入他羣隊。直下便翻身，諸獸皆迴避。毗盧頂上行，生死海中戲。佛祖不知名，眾魔爭敢邇。奇哉此妙門，寂寞無人思。若有發初心，須具大根器。內外絕諸緣，屏心立堅志。譬如人架屋，先須實基址。基實屋無傾，志堅道成易。提箇趙州無，截斷有無意。豎起鐵脊梁，急著眼睛覰。密密與緜緜，絲毫無間棄。譬如人倒懸，念念更無異。日夜苦思量，一心求脫離。不分東與西，寢食都忘記。又如初生兒，呼喚渾不視。用工到那時，如人鑽火燧。漸見黑黃烟，知火必在此。切莫顧危亡，更須加猛利。直待火星飛，通身是𦦨熾。余雖不會禪，也曾恁麼試。只在剎那間，可立而待至。頂門眼豁開，裂破娘生鼻。海竭須彌崩，虗空撲落地。十方賢聖師，盡是眼中刺。微笑與拈花，可煞不知愧。更有葛藤根，一千七百事。嗚呼後代人，盡食他殘饐。若更問如何，拳頭劈口捶。十二時中，四威儀內，寶劍全提，如臨大陣。纔有絲毫念起，當急剉之，一斷永斷，莫令再續。若能如是用工，管取干戈永息，天下太平。有志之士，思之遵之，夜後參前，遞相警勵。此事的要剋日成功，如善射者仰箭射空

Occurrences.Kwic: 事大，及參禪、念佛兩種法門而已。念佛者，只是靠取阿彌陀佛四字話頭，別無他說。若是初心參禪者，恐未有下手處、未有趣向處。然此亦無他說，只是汝諸人各各有箇本來面目，不曾認得這箇本來面目，直下與諸佛同體。你十二時中，語默動靜、行住坐臥，莫不承他恩力。但於此密密體認，即此便是下手處、即此便是趣向處也。便須直下承當，切忌等閑蹉過，發大勇猛、起大精進，要在箭鋒相拄、機筈相投。古人云：一不做，二不休，一拳拳倒黃鶴樓，一踢踢飜鸚鵡洲。有意氣時添意氣，不風流處也風流。果有古人如是作略，則德山與臨濟，與你是同參；釋迦與彌陀，阿曾有兩箇？併將千七百則諸祖機緣，與正法眼藏、涅槃妙心，穿作一串，颺在一邊，然後獨步大方，普告諸人道：丈夫自有通霄路，不向如來行處行。當此之時，則上座望風展拜有分。其或未然，莫恠壓良為賤，再下一箇註脚：世事茫茫沒了期，自家活計猛提撕。落湯螃蠏人人見，投火飛蛾箇箇知。病到始憐身是苦，死來惟有業相隨。浮光幻影須臾過，火急脩行也是遲。如人上山，各自努力。普達實立、副使．脫銕睦爾、副使．買奴海牙、同知．忙哥剌、宣差．馮總管等，率眾官士大夫來師子林設齋，請普說。師云：參禪是向上一著要緊大事。此事曰僧曰俗，人人有分，況是本來具足，全體現成。爭奈世間人往往當面蹉過，不曾去理會。莫道不曾理會，問也不曾問著。正眼看來，誠可憐憫。今日諸公既發此問，畢竟於此事上有大因緣。然此事纔擬說著，便是生死岸頭境界，便是痛心苦口之語。望諸公洗心滌慮，聽之思之。何謂參禪是向上要緊大事？蓋為要明心見性，了生脫死。生死未明，謂之大事。祖師道：參禪只為了生死，生死不了成徒勞。王右軍亦曰：死生亦大矣。豈不痛哉！只為生死事大，故以參禪為向上大事也。何謂生死？公等彼此有身在世，此身既不是諸佛如來金剛不壞之身，又不是純鋼打就、生銕鑄成底堅固之身，乃是四大假合、虗脆浮幻之身，如水上泡，如草頭露。看看髮白齒搖，皮枯面皺，老病無常，朝不保暮。既有生，必有死；既有死，還復生。但不知這回生死落在甚麼道中？此為可痛者也。佛說：三界如火宅，六道如苦輪。汝等從無量劫以至于今，向三界火宅中，東走西走，不知求出路；在六道苦輪裏，東輥西輥，無有暫停時。若欲息苦輪，出火宅，須是了生死；若欲了生死，須是見佛性；若欲見佛性，須是大悟一回；若欲
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1403.xml). Recorded sayings. Tianru closes a warning about impermanence and delayed effort with the pair.

Occurrences.Kwic: 前句後鼓弄人家男女。何故？要且聲不是聲，色不是色，意在鉤頭。僧問：如何是聲不是聲？仁云：喚作色得麼？穿却鼻孔。如何是色不是色？仁云：喚作聲得麼？換却眼睛。僧禮拜。仁云：且道為你說，答你話，若檢點得出，許於佛法中有箇入處，分疎不下。後來雪竇云：本仁也是奇恠，要且貪觀天上，既非聲前色後，從什麼處入？應庵云：雪竇盡其神力，無插手處。只如道：既非聲前色後，從什麼處入？往往十箇有五雙蹉過。還知應庵落處麼？一箭落雙鵰。前輩恁麼互相提唱，不妨綿綿密密控你今人入路。兄弟既名參學，若不於此子細用心與古人相見，將來生死岸頭將何抵擬？山僧却有方便，不見僧問趙州：學人乍入藂林，乞師指示。州云：喫粥了也未？僧云：喫粥了也。州云：洗鉢盂去。僧於此有省。雲門云：且道趙州有指示無指示？若言有，趙州向伊道什麼？若言無，這僧為什麼便禮拜？真如󳭷禪師室中常舉此話，見學者擬下語，便以手掩其口云：歇去。且道真如意作麼生？徑山又不然，有下語者一任下語，只是不得動著。何故？如人上山，各自努力。法語法語示圓上人示圓上人見成公案，豈籍言詮？佇立寄私，垛生招箭。若夢遊區宇底，未免荏苒彷徨，拋家失業，驀忽惻然鼎省，翻得起來，却又不一頓刀刮水洗，心頭隱隱，似記似忘，敗闕愈甚。圓上人拖夢南來，欲求一句以助其省發，予便欲舉須彌槌擊虗空皷，又恐不能呼之。盖睡未稔，去去不能自已，於穿雲渡水時，平步失落，則眼子自開也。此時方可探南山虎穴，透鰻井龍門，先捏定他喉嚨，勿使轉側，方可拔其爪牙，戲其頭角。不尔，遭他一口，喪盡平生，雖曰善因，而招惡果。示源侍者示源侍者昔藥山訪道南嶽，始聞與麼不與麼㹅不得之語，如蚊子上鐵牛，逗到一物不為，閑坐則為；又似箇水上胡蘆子，按也按不住，只管皮膚脫盡，不知真實猶存，引得隨波逐浪。者道：我在藥山三十年，單明此事，種禾却生豆，試點檢他敗闕在什麼處？九上三到，桶底子打脫在木上座手裏，因何却向鰲山店上滯殻迷封？中夜聞豁公撾塗毒之音，返令鹽官色空義洞山過水偈動地放光，是曾郎久參事慢之過耶？西竺初祖呼二祖謂曰：倒却門前剎竿，著八字打開，兩手分付。何故？湧泉道：我四十年猶有走作。香林道：我四十年方打成一片。不出飛猿嶺，目貫九天；不下釣魚山，氣吞四海。備公回公，異代殊方，一狀領過十八上，破家散宅底，因甚老不休歇？無乃徒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1405.xml). Recorded sayings. Shixi ends his own response to the Zhaozhou washing-bowl case by returning responsibility to each practitioner.

Occurrences.Kwic: 水晶宮耳語箇什麼？擊拂子：一葉落，天下秋。小參小參□□□自然等編結制。無上法王有大陀羅尼門，圓而無內，方而無外，無內無外，聖凡普會。若入得此門，則百千三昧門、百千總持門、百千解脫門一時證入，二六時中、四威儀內撞倒燈籠、磕破露柱，且莫麤心好。睦州和尚道：未得箇入頭，須得箇入頭；若得箇入頭，不得孤負老僧。雪峯和尚道：盡大地是個解脫門，把手拽不入。且道古人意在什麼處？今時道流多是自生退屈、自生難易，未證謂證、未得謂得，聞聲被聲礙、見色被色礙、見空被空礙、見山被山礙、見水被水礙、見佛被佛礙、見魔被魔礙，欲得獨步大方，直須高超三界。何謂三界？貪是欲界、嗔是色界、癡是無色界。你一念貪便被水溺、你一念嗔便被火燒、你一念癡便被風飄，若離得者三種，便是出三界外。人聞聲不被聲礙、見色不被色礙、見空不被空礙、見山不被山礙、見水不被水礙、見佛不被佛礙、見魔不被魔礙、說長期短期不被長期短期礙、說安居禁足不被安居禁足礙，一切處自由、一切處無礙。拍禪牀，云：如人上山，各自努力。解夏。黃金真人鐵面具，開眼覰著，凜凜風生。遠山作眉紅杏腮，開得口來，早成話墮。東弗于逮打鼓，南瞻部洲小參。西瞿耶尼安居，北󳬂單越自恣。日月居忉利之上，四禪無風火之災。汝等諸人坐在清凉界中，那裏知得江南兩浙春寒秋熱。喝一喝。結夏。只此處便是妙峯孤頂，龍蛇混雜，凡聖同居。南來者上間安排，北來者下間安著。鼻孔廝拄，赤肉相挨。壁立萬仞底軟似綿團，和泥合水底渾鋼打就。耳裏著得無邊香水海，眼裏著得百億須彌盧。九十日內，佛眼也覰佗不破。只如大通智勝佛，十劫坐道場，因甚不得成佛道？待小溪水逆流，即向汝道。結夏清機，歷掌三十三天撲帝鐘；大用現前，當陽打動關南鼓。衲僧家舉一步，踏翻四大香水海，不喚作禁足得麼？動一念，推倒百億須彌盧，不喚作安居得麼？所以道：若立一塵，野老顰蹙；不立一塵，野老謳歌。百草頭上罷却干戈，閙市門頭識取自己。一月普現一切水，一切水月一月攝。成就八萬四千塵勞門，彈指三生六十劫。冬至。三世諸佛不知有，羊頭車子推明月。狸奴白牯却知有，沒底船兒載曉風。洞明格外真規，漏泄劫前消息。有句無句，如藤倚樹。樹倒藤枯，句歸何處。矮師叔三千里賣却布單即不問，老大溈因甚放下泥盤呵呵大咲。擊拂子。九九陽生第一爻，冬至寒食一百五。歲除，云：日遷月
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1409.xml). Recorded sayings. Yuejiang strikes the Chan seat and speaks the pair after warning against barriers made by sound, form, and thought.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 事大，及參禪、念佛兩種法門而已。念佛者，只是靠取阿彌陀佛四字話頭，別無他說。若是初心參禪者，恐未有下手處、未有趣向處。然此亦無他說，只是汝諸人各各有箇本來面目，不曾認得這箇本來面目，直下與諸佛同體。你十二時中，語默動靜、行住坐臥，莫不承他恩力。但於此密密體認，即此便是下手處、即此便是趣向處也。便須直下承當，切忌等閑蹉過，發大勇猛、起大精進，要在箭鋒相拄、機筈相投。古人云：一不做，二不休，一拳拳倒黃鶴樓，一踢踢飜鸚鵡洲。有意氣時添意氣，不風流處也風流。果有古人如是作略，則德山與臨濟，與你是同參；釋迦與彌陀，阿曾有兩箇？併將千七百則諸祖機緣，與正法眼藏、涅槃妙心，穿作一串，颺在一邊，然後獨步大方，普告諸人道：丈夫自有通霄路，不向如來行處行。當此之時，則上座望風展拜有分。其或未然，莫恠壓良為賤，再下一箇註脚：世事茫茫沒了期，自家活計猛提撕。落湯螃蠏人人見，投火飛蛾箇箇知。病到始憐身是苦，死來惟有業相隨。浮光幻影須臾過，火急脩行也是遲。如人上山，各自努力。普達實立、副使．脫銕睦爾、副使．買奴海牙、同知．忙哥剌、宣差．馮總管等，率眾官士大夫來師子林設齋，請普說。師云：參禪是向上一著要緊大事。此事曰僧曰俗，人人有分，況是本來具足，全體現成。爭奈世間人往往當面蹉過，不曾去理會。莫道不曾理會，問也不曾問著。正眼看來，誠可憐憫。今日諸公既發此問，畢竟於此事上有大因緣。然此事纔擬說著，便是生死岸頭境界，便是痛心苦口之語。望諸公洗心滌慮，聽之思之。何謂參禪是向上要緊大事？蓋為要明心見性，了生脫死。生死未明，謂之大事。祖師道：參禪只為了生死，生死不了成徒勞。王右軍亦曰：死生亦大矣。豈不痛哉！只為生死事大，故以參禪為向上大事也。何謂生死？公等彼此有身在世，此身既不是諸佛如來金剛不壞之身，又不是純鋼打就、生銕鑄成底堅固之身，乃是四大假合、虗脆浮幻之身，如水上泡，如草頭露。看看髮白齒搖，皮枯面皺，老病無常，朝不保暮。既有生，必有死；既有死，還復生。但不知這回生死落在甚麼道中？此為可痛者也。佛說：三界如火宅，六道如苦輪。汝等從無量劫以至于今，向三界火宅中，東走西走，不知求出路；在六道苦輪裏，東輥西輥，無有暫停時。若欲息苦輪，出火宅，須是了生死；若欲了生死，須是見佛性；若欲見佛性，須是大悟一回；若欲

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 前句後鼓弄人家男女。何故？要且聲不是聲，色不是色，意在鉤頭。僧問：如何是聲不是聲？仁云：喚作色得麼？穿却鼻孔。如何是色不是色？仁云：喚作聲得麼？換却眼睛。僧禮拜。仁云：且道為你說，答你話，若檢點得出，許於佛法中有箇入處，分疎不下。後來雪竇云：本仁也是奇恠，要且貪觀天上，既非聲前色後，從什麼處入？應庵云：雪竇盡其神力，無插手處。只如道：既非聲前色後，從什麼處入？往往十箇有五雙蹉過。還知應庵落處麼？一箭落雙鵰。前輩恁麼互相提唱，不妨綿綿密密控你今人入路。兄弟既名參學，若不於此子細用心與古人相見，將來生死岸頭將何抵擬？山僧却有方便，不見僧問趙州：學人乍入藂林，乞師指示。州云：喫粥了也未？僧云：喫粥了也。州云：洗鉢盂去。僧於此有省。雲門云：且道趙州有指示無指示？若言有，趙州向伊道什麼？若言無，這僧為什麼便禮拜？真如󳭷禪師室中常舉此話，見學者擬下語，便以手掩其口云：歇去。且道真如意作麼生？徑山又不然，有下語者一任下語，只是不得動著。何故？如人上山，各自努力。法語法語示圓上人示圓上人見成公案，豈籍言詮？佇立寄私，垛生招箭。若夢遊區宇底，未免荏苒彷徨，拋家失業，驀忽惻然鼎省，翻得起來，却又不一頓刀刮水洗，心頭隱隱，似記似忘，敗闕愈甚。圓上人拖夢南來，欲求一句以助其省發，予便欲舉須彌槌擊虗空皷，又恐不能呼之。盖睡未稔，去去不能自已，於穿雲渡水時，平步失落，則眼子自開也。此時方可探南山虎穴，透鰻井龍門，先捏定他喉嚨，勿使轉側，方可拔其爪牙，戲其頭角。不尔，遭他一口，喪盡平生，雖曰善因，而招惡果。示源侍者示源侍者昔藥山訪道南嶽，始聞與麼不與麼㹅不得之語，如蚊子上鐵牛，逗到一物不為，閑坐則為；又似箇水上胡蘆子，按也按不住，只管皮膚脫盡，不知真實猶存，引得隨波逐浪。者道：我在藥山三十年，單明此事，種禾却生豆，試點檢他敗闕在什麼處？九上三到，桶底子打脫在木上座手裏，因何却向鰲山店上滯殻迷封？中夜聞豁公撾塗毒之音，返令鹽官色空義洞山過水偈動地放光，是曾郎久參事慢之過耶？西竺初祖呼二祖謂曰：倒却門前剎竿，著八字打開，兩手分付。何故？湧泉道：我四十年猶有走作。香林道：我四十年方打成一片。不出飛猿嶺，目貫九天；不下釣魚山，氣吞四海。備公回公，異代殊方，一狀領過十八上，破家散宅底，因甚老不休歇？無乃徒

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 水晶宮耳語箇什麼？擊拂子：一葉落，天下秋。小參小參□□□自然等編結制。無上法王有大陀羅尼門，圓而無內，方而無外，無內無外，聖凡普會。若入得此門，則百千三昧門、百千總持門、百千解脫門一時證入，二六時中、四威儀內撞倒燈籠、磕破露柱，且莫麤心好。睦州和尚道：未得箇入頭，須得箇入頭；若得箇入頭，不得孤負老僧。雪峯和尚道：盡大地是個解脫門，把手拽不入。且道古人意在什麼處？今時道流多是自生退屈、自生難易，未證謂證、未得謂得，聞聲被聲礙、見色被色礙、見空被空礙、見山被山礙、見水被水礙、見佛被佛礙、見魔被魔礙，欲得獨步大方，直須高超三界。何謂三界？貪是欲界、嗔是色界、癡是無色界。你一念貪便被水溺、你一念嗔便被火燒、你一念癡便被風飄，若離得者三種，便是出三界外。人聞聲不被聲礙、見色不被色礙、見空不被空礙、見山不被山礙、見水不被水礙、見佛不被佛礙、見魔不被魔礙、說長期短期不被長期短期礙、說安居禁足不被安居禁足礙，一切處自由、一切處無礙。拍禪牀，云：如人上山，各自努力。解夏。黃金真人鐵面具，開眼覰著，凜凜風生。遠山作眉紅杏腮，開得口來，早成話墮。東弗于逮打鼓，南瞻部洲小參。西瞿耶尼安居，北󳬂單越自恣。日月居忉利之上，四禪無風火之災。汝等諸人坐在清凉界中，那裏知得江南兩浙春寒秋熱。喝一喝。結夏。只此處便是妙峯孤頂，龍蛇混雜，凡聖同居。南來者上間安排，北來者下間安著。鼻孔廝拄，赤肉相挨。壁立萬仞底軟似綿團，和泥合水底渾鋼打就。耳裏著得無邊香水海，眼裏著得百億須彌盧。九十日內，佛眼也覰佗不破。只如大通智勝佛，十劫坐道場，因甚不得成佛道？待小溪水逆流，即向汝道。結夏清機，歷掌三十三天撲帝鐘；大用現前，當陽打動關南鼓。衲僧家舉一步，踏翻四大香水海，不喚作禁足得麼？動一念，推倒百億須彌盧，不喚作安居得麼？所以道：若立一塵，野老顰蹙；不立一塵，野老謳歌。百草頭上罷却干戈，閙市門頭識取自己。一月普現一切水，一切水月一月攝。成就八萬四千塵勞門，彈指三生六十劫。冬至。三世諸佛不知有，羊頭車子推明月。狸奴白牯却知有，沒底船兒載曉風。洞明格外真規，漏泄劫前消息。有句無句，如藤倚樹。樹倒藤枯，句歸何處。矮師叔三千里賣却布單即不問，老大溈因甚放下泥盤呵呵大咲。擊拂子。九九陽生第一爻，冬至寒食一百五。歲除，云：日遷月

Occurrences.Kwic: 保福拈問長慶：「嵒頭平生出世，有什摩言教過於德山，便道『猶較些子』？」長慶舉師示眾云：「若是得意底人，自解作活計。舉措悉皆索索底，時長恬恬底。觸物則傳，意在傳處。住則鏟住，去則鏟去。須於欲去不去、欲住不住處體會。不執物，不據物。不同窒塞人緊把著事不解傳得，恰似死人把玉擩玉相似。縱然傳得，直到驢年有什摩用處？且愧伊向這裏湊泊，不別運為。訝將去，鑽將去，研將去，直教透過，直教通徹。不見道『如人學射，久久方中』？」有人問：「中時如何？」師云：「莫不識痛痒摩？」保福云：「今日非唯舉話。」慶云：「是什摩心行？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (B/B25/B25n0144.xml). Zutang Ji (Anthology from the Patriarchs’ Hall). The Patriarchs' Hall anthology raises Baofu asking Changqing what Yantou could teach beyond Deshan's declaration that his school has no words or teaching to give. Changqing quotes Yantou's instruction to move freely without clinging to things or being obstructed by them, ending with learning archery and hitting the target only after long practice. Asked what happens when one hits, Yantou replies with recognizing pain and itching. Baofu then says the exchange is more than merely quoting a case. The exact pair belongs to Yantou's quoted instruction. Its patient practice is joined to responsive contact, not a guarantee that repetition of a fixed movement alone produces realization.

Occurrences.Kwic: 示濟禪人參禪人須參活句，莫參死句。何謂活句？只如僧問趙州：「狗子還有佛性也無？」州云：「無。」又問：「一切眾生皆有佛性，因甚狗子無佛性？」州云：「他有業識在。」這便是活句。這僧向活句上問，趙州又向活句上答。你如今要這一則公案分曉，只就業識紛飛處看。業識與麼紛飛，如何是無業識田地？佛性現成，如何得見佛性與佛祖一般？如人學射，久久方中，所謂得之於心，應之於手。卻不可滯在有上，滯在有上便同眾生；又不可滯在無上，教中謂之相違；又不可滯在非有非無上，教中謂之戲論。總不落階級，不涉廉纖，著著有出身之路，始到得活句邊，猶未取得老趙州性命在。且道老趙州性命作麼生取？不見五祖演和尚云：「趙州露刃劍，寒霜光焰焰，更擬問如何，分身作兩段。」你且道是死句？是活句？參。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB273.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Qianyan. Qianyan Yuanzhang instructs practitioner Ji to investigate living rather than dead sentences, raising Zhaozhou's refusal of Buddha-nature to a dog and the explanation of active conditioning. Look precisely where that conditioning flies about, he says: how is the ground without it and how can Buddha-nature be seen? He gives the archery pair and the relation between gaining something in the heart and answering through the hand. Yet one must not remain with existence, nonexistence, or neither, and even reaching a living sentence has not seized Zhaozhou's life. The headword is Qianyan's present comparison for sustained examination; its surrounding prohibitions prevent practice from becoming a fixed conceptual position.

Senses.Explanation: Like someone learning archery, only after long practice does one hit the target. The Patriarchs' Hall anthology raises Baofu asking Changqing what Yantou could teach beyond Deshan's declaration that his school has no words or teaching to give. Changqing quotes Yantou's instruction to move freely without clinging to things or being obstructed by them, ending with learning archery and hitting the target only after long practice. SearchAliases: drinking water knows cold and warmth
Senses.Explanation: In these records, drinking water supplies a recurrent comparison for knowledge reported by the drinker: cold and warmth are known by the person who drinks. Literally, “like a person drinking water.” In the Chan record the phrase normally continues “knowing cold and warmth oneself.” Its Zen-specific use is as a stock comparison for knowledge that the person concerned reports from his own encounter rather than receives as another person's verbal description. In the Huineng and Huiming encounter, Huiming responds after Huineng's question about his face before his parents were born: “like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself.” Dahui says that at this point it is like drinking water and knowing its temperature oneself, and adds, “unless one has personally verified and personally understood, one can then see it.” The Record of the Mirror of the School frames a question with “understanding the way and clarifying the school are like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself—how can their manner be spoken?”, and elsewhere pairs the comparison with “only verification knows; it is difficult to measure.” Poshan states the same deviation in domestic language: “only each person understands inside his own belly”, followed by the water comparison. Thus the corpus retains the ordinary act of drinking but makes the drinker's private knowledge of cold or warmth its recurring Chan predicate.

Senses.PreferredTarget: As with drinking water, one knows its warmth or coldness oneself
AlternateTargets: Only the person who drinks the water knows whether it is warm or cold
SearchAliases: drinking water knows hot and cold
know for oneself like water temperature
Senses.Note: As a person who drinks water knows its warmth or coldness directly, so a student must discern the matter for himself. These masters use the older simile to test claimed understanding, direct a householder's inquiry, or urge care in everyday conditions. It does not mean that all responses are beyond discussion; the simile asks for personal verification.

Senses.Explanation: ‘As with drinking water, one knows its warmth or coldness oneself’ makes direct discernment as ordinary as feeling the temperature of a drink. Masters use it to press listeners beyond repeating an answer that belongs to someone else. Linquan applies the simile after questioning a verbal assessment of his case comment. Kongyin asks listeners to check themselves amid changing conditions rather than pretend to a settled state. Poshan says people share the same hall and senses, yet each must become clear for himself. Yingshan tells a householder to carry out his instruction until the matter is known without asking another person. Binya uses the line with cold and heat before a furnace address. Faxi writes that a teacher cannot pass this recognition by description and urges direct realization.

Occurrences.Kwic: 示眾云：老僧二十年前住三峯庵時，有魏府興化長老來問，權借一問以為影草時如何？老僧當時機思遲鈍，道不得為伊，致得箇話頭奇特，不敢辜負伊。他云：想和尚答這話不得，不如禮拜了退。如今思量，當時不消道箇何必。後遣化主到魏府興化，化問：和尚住三峰庵時，老僧問伊話對不得，如今道得也未？主舉前話，化云：雲居二十年，只道得箇何必？興化即不然，爭如箇道不必？三聖云：雲居二十年，道得底猶較興化半月程。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp. Yunju Daoying tells the assembly that twenty years earlier Xinghua Cunjiang asked to borrow a question as a probe. Yunju could not answer, and Xinghua suggested he simply bow and withdraw. Thinking back, Yunju now proposes that a 'why bother?' would have done then. A later messenger carries this to Xinghua, who says Yunju has spent twenty years only arriving at 'why bother?' and offers 'no need' instead. Sansheng says Yunju is still half a month behind Xinghua. Senses.PreferredTarget: Now I would like another blow; who will deliver it?
AlternateTargets: I still want one more beating; who will lay a hand on me?
SearchAliases: Linji another blow who will deliver it
Senses.Note: The local challenge and the current teacher's response govern the reading; quoted evaluations are not universal factual claims.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟曰：「夫為法者不避喪身失命，我於黃檗先師處，三度問佛法的的大意，三度被打，如蒿枝拂相似，如今更思一頓，誰為下手？」時有僧出曰：「某甲下手。」師度與拄杖，僧擬接，師便打。憶得當年中毒來，懷抱何曾一打開，今日人前弄牙爪，擒龍捉虎活生埋。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. Linji Yixuan recalls asking Huangbo three times for the essential meaning of the Buddha's teaching and being struck three times, now likening the blows to a brushing with mugwort twigs. Saying that someone seeking the teaching does not avoid losing body and life, he asks who will give him another beating. A monk volunteers; Linji offers the staff but strikes as the monk reaches to take it. Feiyin Tongrong raises this case and answers in verse with poison received long ago, an unopened embrace, and the display of fangs and claws that captures dragons and tigers. Feiyin's forceful images appraise the old blows' continuing operation; the exact request remains Linji's quoted speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟遠祖云：「我二十年前在黃檗先師處三度問佛法的的大意，三度被打，如蒿枝拂相似，如今更思一頓，誰為下手？」時有僧出云：「某甲下手。」濟度與拄杖，僧擬接，濟便打。蓋其平生徹證超出過量，不與時輩合水和泥者比，比便是正脈、便是源流、便是耀古騰今大人境界也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. Baichi Xingyuan quotes Linji's recollection, the request for another beating, the volunteer and the blow delivered before he takes the staff. Baichi then explicitly praises Linji's lifetime of thorough verification as beyond ordinary measure, contrasting it with contemporaries who mix everything into mud. He calls it the true pulse and source, a great person's domain shining across past and present. The headword is an example supporting Baichi's evaluative claim about lived realization, not a request from Baichi to the audience for corporal punishment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟示眾云：「我在先師處，三度問佛法的的大意，三度被打，如蒿枝拂相似。如今更思一頓，誰為下手？」時，有僧出，云：「某為下手。」師拈棒度與僧，僧擬接棒，師便打。拈云：「臨濟迸富連貧，罄家一蕩，猶向百尺竿頭弄線，卻令者僧纔擬搆望，便與捺倒。雖然，未免殺人犯手，被這僧忍行苦肉，誰知臨濟直至而今遭人簡點。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB205.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Jieweizhou. Jieweizhou Xingzhou raises the same exchange but complicates Linji's apparent command of it. He describes Linji pouring out his riches and playing a line at the top of a hundred-foot pole, only to push the monk down as soon as he reaches. Yet Linji cannot avoid getting his own hands implicated: the monk's patient acceptance of bodily suffering leaves Linji open to criticism even now. The exact request is Linji's; the present comment refuses to make the subsequent strike a victory beyond appraisal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 晚參。舉臨濟如今更思一頓，誰為下手因緣？師曰：「人人盡道臨濟乃握閫外威權，者僧未具透關眼目，殊不知只消者僧道箇某甲下手，臨濟便膽戰心驚、手忙腳亂。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB390.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chulin of Beijing. Chulin Shangrui raises the case by the headword and reverses its familiar assessment. Everyone says Linji commanded authority beyond the fortress and that the monk lacked the eye to penetrate the barrier; Chulin says they fail to see that the monk's simple 'I will strike' was enough to make Linji tremble and lose his composure. This is Chulin's deliberately contrary judgment of the old turn, not a report that the quoted monk actually struck Linji or a reading endorsed by all the retained teachers.

Senses.Explanation: The enthronement gauntlet that turns a new abbot's authority into a question demanding an instant display. Baiyu Jingsi, entering the abbot's quarters at Longhua where the old master ran his forge — bone-tapping, Buddha-smelting, nail-pulling — asks how this unworthy one will deploy, cracks his staff, and tells the hall to watch the command take effect; Guxue Zhenzhe, taking the room at Cuiyan where the ancestors pulled nails and loosened bonds for lake-and-sea monks, asks how Zhe deploys there and lets the seven-foot black rattan decide for you; Wanru Tongwei, taking the room at Caoshan, rules that Magadha's closed door and Vimalakirti's silence, though they cut off past and present, are unfit for the teaching, asks how this mountain monk deploys, and passes even the iron-browed copper heads only through the red furnace; and Jieweizhou Xingzhou, before the seat of the new Puji temple in the capital, asks how the new Puji will deploy, shouts once, and mounts the seat. Muchen Daomin, in the ceremonial-robe turn of his Tiantong enthronement, pictures shedding the jewels for hides and entering the market basket, asks how to deploy just then, and would overturn seas and ridges to find one who knows; Tianyin Yuanxiu, at the Yixing donors' xiaocan, grants heaven covers, earth generates, the king blesses, and ministers repay the state — then asks what the patch-robed one does with it, and the young Yulin, waiting at his side, overturns the incense table and cuts off the tongues of the world; Qiran Chaozhi, after quoting Dahui's bathing-the-buddha address, rules that for the supreme device the patch-robed monk's grip has not yet been dreamed of, then asks how after all to deploy — the cart is not pushed sideways, the truth not bent; and Lianfeng Su, having fallen as a young man into the old masters' pit and still unable to leap out with all his strength, asks the senior seat Langxuan how one deploys when one cannot get out, raising his whisk: flour is milled where the wheat grew, and songs must be sung in the emperor's home town.

Senses.Explanation: What is it when both person and environment are taken away? (如何是人境兩俱奪) is the question form of the third member in a recurrent four-part sequence: the person taken away but not the environment, the environment taken away but not the person, both taken away, and neither taken away. The records do not supply one stock answer. Linji Yixuan answers with ‘news cut off from Bing and Fen, dwelling alone in one region’; Yinyuan Longqi puts down his staff; Tianyin Yuanxiu tells the questioner to stand aside and, in another recorded exchange, says that there is neither one who explains the teaching nor one who listens. The retained lamp recension records Sanjiao Zhisong answering, ‘a headless toad points a foot at the sky.’ The stable lexical unit is the question and its place in the four-part sequence, not any one response.

Senses.Explanation: The stock public-interview demand for the central point of the buddhas' teaching. Daolin answers Bai Juyi with 'do no evils; carry out the many goods'; Qingyuan Xingsi asks an unnamed monk the price of rice in Luling; Linji Yixuan shouts at one unnamed monk and raises the whisk before striking another; Zhaozhou Congshen tells an unnamed monk to pay his respects and then cuts off the attempted continuation. When Ding Shangzuo asks, Linji leaves the Chan seat, seizes Ding, slaps him, and pushes him away. Xuedou Chongxian answers another unnamed monk with 'five-colored auspicious clouds.' The repeated formula is one public demand, while its recorded replies range across maxim, counter-question, shout, implement, image, and bodily action. The records supply no single answer shared by all these exchanges.

Senses.Explanation: This is an unnamed monk’s question in Dongshan Liangjie’s heat-and-cold case: where can one go to avoid both conditions? Dongshan first directs an unnamed questioning monk to a place without heat or cold, then answers the request to identify it: ‘When cold, let the cold kill you; when hot, let the heat kill you.’ The Blue Cliff Record and later collections transmit this same exchange.

Senses.PreferredTarget: what did Bodhidharma come from the West for?
AlternateTargets: what is the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West?
SearchAliases: why did Bodhidharma come from India
meaning of the ancestral teacher's arrival
Senses.Explanation: “What did Bodhidharma come from the West for?” is a fixed public-interview question about what the ancestral teacher's west-to-east coming amounted to. The question is a lexical object in its own right, separate from the sharply different answers and actions that follow it. An unnamed monk asks Zhaozhou Congshen and receives the cypress in the courtyard; multiple later works preserve that inherited family, but it counts as one encounter. Elsewhere an unnamed monk receives Chan Master Dawei's promise to answer after turning around at Fanxian Mountain. Ding Shangzuo asks it and Linji Yixuan descends, seizes him, and demands that he speak; Longya Judun asks Linji and is told to pass over the Chan bench before Linji strikes. Wuzu Fayan actively reuses the formula while pressing Yuanwu Keqin about the cypress, and Fayun Xiu proposes “verbal fall” as the reply if someone asks him. The varied responses establish the stability of the question, not a menu of meanings for it.
Senses.Note: Bodhidharma is the ancestral teacher conventionally invoked by this formula. Cypress, bench, blow, demand, and other responses belong to their own turns and must not be folded into the question's translation.

Senses.Explanation: A questioner asks the respondent to demonstrate the first of the three essentials associated with Linji's three mysteries and three essentials. Across six independent records, the question appears inside a serial public exchange: the questioner asks for each mystery and then each essential in order. The replies differ sharply, including 'myriad differences are all illuminated in one light,' news of an amnesty, a returning night boat, 'opening your mouth is already laughable,' Yama's karmic mirror, and a wooden hawk flying through the sky. The stable dictionary unit is therefore the test-question itself, not any one reply.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, this asks, ‘Where do the buddhas emerge?’ It is a stable encounter question rather than the name of a place. Yuanwu Keqin records the unnamed monk's question to Yunmen Wenyan and Yunmen's answer, ‘East Mountain walks on water.’ In Dahui Zonggao's recollection, Yuanwu raises that exchange and gives a different answer: ‘A warm wind comes from the south; a slight coolness enters the palace halls.’ The Five Lamps Compendium preserves a separate exchange with Master Lingkan of Western Sichuan, who answers, ‘Emergence has nothing to do with buddhas; when spring comes, grass greens by itself.’ The differing answers do not change the wording or grammatical referent of the question.

Senses.Explanation: What is the phrase that threads through the truth-body — the school's standing demand for the word that goes through rather than points, asked of Yunmen and answered with the Dipper, then ruled, re-answered, versed, and smuggled for five hundred years. The origin, in Yunmen Wenyan's own catechism. Question after question runs the gauntlet — the Yunmen sword: the ancestor; the birthplace of all buddhas: ask me another; the white ox in the open: the confronting cue that changes no road. Then: what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? The master: hide the body in the Dipper. And next after: what is the original school? Not asking, not answering. Dahui Zonggao raises the exchange in the hall and rules on it: the old man of Yunmen, answering thus, answered only the truth-body phrase — he did not answer the phrase that threads through. If today someone asked Jingshan, what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body — I would tell him: a night-market opened in a midge's eye, a swing swung on a great tiger's tongue. And Miyun Yuanwu, raising both at the Tongxuan temple, turns it a third way: if anyone asks me what the threading-through phrase is — a staff across the spine on the spot; even if he does not understand, I guarantee he will not forget it for a whole eternity. The other line of the family: a monk asks Bajiao Huiqing, what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? Bajiao: first, you may not ask; second, you may not rest. The monk: I do not understand. Bajiao: come a third time and I will meet you. Touzi Yiqing verses it: ask not of Vimalakirti lying ill within the city; Vulture Peak idly shuts away its light. To cross the flowing sands is without difficulty — only do not hear the oriole crying in that grove. And Daxiu Zhu, raising the same at the Buddha-birthday hall and versing: not asking, not resting — the truth-body is not on the tip of the tongue; but let the third coming bring the meeting, and it will run the Guishan water-buffalo to death. Yuejiang Zhengyin, in his own hall catechism at Dianshan: what is the birthplace of all buddhas? Is the Dianshan lake full yet? What is the blow-hair sword? Dust rising from a well-bottom. What is the white ox in the open? Hewing the forehead, gazing toward Caoxi. And what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? That smuggler of private salt. Then he turns on the assembly: under white sun and blue sky, dreamers with open eyes are as hemp and millet — bring me the dream-thing to look at. You see me talk thus and say the old man talks in his sleep — but when you are not dreaming, what is the thing before your eyes? And Eryin Mi, picking old cases: the elder Fulang, meeting the questioner's line at Yunmen's gate — the master hid the body in the Dipper; Fulang could not fathom it and pressed further. Yunmen gripped him: Speak, speak! Fulang hesitated; the master pushed him away and gave a verse — the cloud-gate tower sheers off the low white clouds; fish in rushing water dare not rest; entering the gate, your seeing was already known — why trouble to lift the rutting mud again? Fulang woke whole. Gripped and pushed away, rolling whole-bodied through the grass; the verse retold, the tongue dragging on the ground — yet the elder who opened an eye right there, says Eryin, is still only a lacquer bucket.

Senses.Explanation: What is the Way? is a recurring public-interview question. Zhaozhou Congshen asks Nanquan Puyuan and receives “ordinary mind is the Way.” Li Ao asks Yaoshan Weiyan, who points upward and then to a water jar. A quoted monk asks Shitou Xiqian and receives “wood,” while another quoted monk asks Xingshan Weikuan and receives “a fine mountain.” The same question opens distinct encounters with unlike answers.

Tianyin Yuanxiu owns the retained deployment: raises the meeting of the two old worthies, the one who gave tiger cries and the one who laughed and called him a master, and says whoever recognizes the full workings before their eyes needs no how-or-what but enters with the single blade, while a blind turtle and lame turtle cannot carry it on.

Senses.Explanation: Two questions folded into one, and the masters who bar the asking at the gate. Xinghua Cunjiang opens his hall with incense for his late teacher Linji and tells the assembly that today he asks no how-or-what but bids them enter with the single blade, Ciming Chuyuan rules that just going like that is already too much and any how-or-what merely kneads mud into water, Foyan Qingyuan contrasts the ancients' painstaking answers with descendants who shout the moment you enter the gate, no how-or-what at all, only afraid you might not understand, Wu'an Puning sizes up the half-believing who ask one line today and one tomorrow and still come asking their how-or-what, solemn and courtly, and Qianyan Yuanzhang has the drum sound, the assembly gather, host and guest change places, and no one asks how-or-what, the enjoyment ready-made as it is. Sanfeng Hanyue bathes the Buddha and promises a ladle of foul water in advance to any of them who stirs lips and tongue and steps forward to ask a how-or-what, Poshan Haiming traces Daruma's words and Linji's blows to the grant of the sacred seat straight to the common man with no how-or-what, and that as knowing where it hurts, Miyun Yuanwu at the furnace opening bids whoever transcends buddha and ancestor skip the how-or-what and meet the Tongxuan staff, Feiyin Tongrong warns the retreat assembly that in the red furnace of neither releasing nor holding, to be about to how-or-what is already to lose body and life, and Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the two old worthies' tiger-roar meeting and says whoever recognizes it needs no how-or-what but enters with the single blade.

Entries.SourceTerm: 如來禪許師弟會，祖師禪未夢見在

Senses.PreferredTarget: I grant that you understand Tathagata Chan; you have not even dreamed of ancestral Chan
SearchAliases: i grant that you understand tathagata chan; you have not even dreamed of ancestral chan
Senses.Note: Yangshan tells Xiangyan that he understands Tathagata Chan but has not dreamed of ancestral Chan. Xiangyan answers with another verse, after which Yangshan changes his verdict. Poshan and Hanyue discuss what this turn tests; Huanchu pushes back by denying even the first allowance. Yushan calls Yangshan's remark sleep-talk, while Jianru and Zhanran return to the sequence of probing and reply. The saying is a provisional challenge inside a continuing encounter.

Senses.Explanation: The grief-measure of the great affair: a mourning as raw as a parent's death, required while the matter is unset and still required once it is settled. Muzhou Daoming speaks the root hall instruction itself — the great affair unset, mourn like this; the great affair settled, still mourn like this — and the anthology keeps the later questioners circling it; Yunwai Xingze rings it as the small-meeting bell for time running out; Yulin Tongxiu lifts the staff, credits the old worthies with the saying, and presses why the settled affair still grieves; and Binya Jian opens a memorial hall service by making the whole pair the sermon before asking the assembly why the settled half mourns. Yezhu Fuhui hangs the pair at the head of a hall address and levels it with a road verse; Chaozong Tongren sings it into paired verse for the patron's memorial service, rootless confusion and idle furniture both under the same grief; Eryin Mi swaps the frame to the great way and voices the double mourning beside his own peaks; and Konggu Daocheng, recounting three years of standing at cliffs and walking open ground, holds the old formula as the thread of the whole striving.

Mi'an Xianjie teaches that when mind and dharmas are both forgotten it is like drumming the poison drum, all who hear it perish, and again like a great mass of fire, near it and it scorches your face, so that those who wake stand as buddhas on the spot and those lost revolve for eternal kalpas, Ying'an Tanhua runs Muzhou's ready-made case, Zhizhi's one finger, Bimo's raised trident down the whole line of the old worthies, each held up at its exact aching point like a great mass of fire that none dare approach, approach it and it scorches your face, again like the golden-winged bird splitting the sea to swallow the dragon outright, Zhongfeng Mingben warns students not to smear their own clean field with fox spittle by taking such sayings for some kind of principle, since the ancients' opening of the mouth was like a great mass of fire and a great wind-wheel with nowhere to touch down, and like a sharp sword drawn casually to cut the life-root, and Xueqiao Yuanxin opens the retreat's end saying it was all for the one great matter under each person's heels, unclear like a great mass of fire with no coolness to be had, naming himself the white-taking thief standing on one foot at the crest of ten thousand fathoms. Wuyi Yuanlai tells his cousins that getting it is like a great mass of fire and not getting it is also like a great mass of fire, on the high mountain no roosting birds, in the deep water fine fish, before granting that Boyan too is just ladling at an empty sound, Yongjue Yuanxian grades Fenyang's three phrases as like a great mass of fire, near it you may not go, turn your back and it is not fire, Miyun Yuanwu opens the furnace with prajna as a great mass of fire, propound on it and it scorches your face, then raps his staff for the one who does not shun the flame at the furnace, and Baichi Xingyuan sets the pivots of the buddhas and the handles of the patriarchs strewn before him like a great mass of fire, where calling it a staff is a miss and not calling it a staff is a turning away.

Senses.Explanation: Like heaven overspreading: the total reach of the one thing — Deshan's stick for one master, the great matter under everyone's heels for another, and the bare answer to a hundred-million Wenshus. Fenyang Shanzhao sets the Song root in verse: true gold from the Li river weighs no more, road gravel no less — heaven overspreading, earth upbearing — and under that roof the utterly poor son comes home while the misjudging crowd quarrels over him; Yuanwu Keqin, at the request of the transport official Liu, works it through the wisdom-light that breaks the dark of birth-and-death and the diamond sword that cuts the fetters: where the break-through happens one thought is not more, and in the use of it the whole body is eye — until it comes to heaven overspreading and earth upbearing, sun shining on all, wind cooling all, not one thread shifted, not one mote screening; Dahui Zonggao diagnoses the racing mind the teaching calls restlessness, and then plants what none of it touches: under each person's heels a stretch of the great matter that neither sinks nor races — like heaven overspreading, like earth upbearing; before there was a world this great matter already was, and when the world breaks, it will not have stirred a hair-tip; Tian'an Sheng, pressed on the one true Wenshu — no second Wenshu, so why a hundred-million Wenshus? — answers with the bare couplet: heaven overspreading, earth upbearing, and when the disciple laughs at Kashyapa's silence he lets the bystanders fall over laughing. Chaozong Tongren, at the evening assembly of Wen-tao hermitage in Shucheng, rules what a lineage master must do: Deshan's stick at the gate is heaven overspreading, Linji's shout at the gate is earth upbearing — never dropping to second or third, never cheating anyone's sons and daughters, while those who guide by capacity have the three vehicles and twelve divisions instead; Daxiu Zhu, watching the gate dwindle, refuses to play teacher for pleasure: a great man standing between heaven and earth must plant his body and walk the way — like heaven overspreading, like earth upbearing — the rain of the teaching falling equal, the three grasses and two trees all moistened; Gusu Zun asks the assembly whether they see it through: this one thing is not less in the commoner nor more in the sage — see straight through and it stands like heaven overspreading and earth upbearing, with no facing or backing, no near and far; Tianyi Juxiang, against branch-chasing after a painted cake, turns it home: the ten thousand things are the light of mind, the conditions announce the nature — know the one mind and the ten thousand things are clear, like heaven overspreading and earth upbearing, sun, moon, and stars, rivers and sacred peaks, down to the whole treasury of forms, all showing forth within it, never lacking one point.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舊話。青州衫重七斤，廬陵米作麼價？謝勤維那、虎維那泉南持鉢歸，上堂：海外同歸用亦同，靈山有此兩雲峰。萬人叢裡高標上，只貴重論蓋代功。中秋，上堂。圓處圓還缺，缺處缺還圓，人爭看今日，月只是常年。南泉拂袖便行，鼓山拂袖歸眾，說甚衲僧門下，直是重處偏墜，薄處先穿。謝書記上堂，舉雲門因僧問：如何是清淨法身？門云：六不収。後來圓悟云：雲門只道得一半。若問道林：如何是清淨法身？只向他道：一不立。師云：圓悟與麼也只道得八成，靈隱今日更資一路，又要二大老兩得相見，妙處無私，辭鋒可驗，十字縱橫，文不加點。上堂：色心不二，彼我無差。以拂子擊禪牀，云：主山高，案山低，森羅顯煥，萬象樅然。更待截鶴續鳧，夷岳盈壑，何啻白雲千里萬里？至節，上堂。一年復一年，一冬復一冬，海水知天寒，枯桑知天風。諸人了了，常知甚處是如如不動？拍禪牀，云：一陽生也。上堂：大智發於心，且莫草草匇匇。於心何處尋？果然古人與麼，大似大開口了合不得。聖節，上堂。十方國土中，惟有一乘法。如天普蓋，似地普擎。野老謳歌，漁人舞棹。只如蒲團上打坐，佛殿裡燒香。又且如何？恩大難酬。除夜，小參。道無蹊徑，平地裡礙却潼關，其數河沙；法離見聞，劒刃上翻得身來，萬中無一。除是不存窠臼、不立孤危，戢玄機未兆已前進得一步，家貧難辦素食；藏冥運即化之際突得一句，事忙不及草書。三九二十七，菩提涅槃，真如解脫。睦州陳蒲鞋。倒腹傾膓，猶欠一著。如何是那一著？角吹新歲曲，梅放去年花。復舉：丹霞一日與龐居士行次，見一泓水，士以手指云：得恁麼也還辨不出？霞云：灼然是辨不出。士乃戽水潑霞三下，霞云：莫恁麼！莫恁麼！士云：須恁麼！須恁麼！霞戽水潑士三下，士云：正當恁麼時堪作甚麼？霞云：無外物。士云：得便宜者少。霞不語。士云：誰是落便宜者？師云：莫恁麼！須恁麼！得便宜！落便宜！戽水相潑，小兒子戲。上堂：智門蓮花，趙州庭栢。不用低頭，思量難得。上堂：吾本來茲土，傳法救迷情。面皮厚多少，一花開五葉。結果自然成，蕪纇清平盡。西天此土之鐵，不能鑄此一錯。且諸人向甚處見祖師？佛涅槃，上堂，舉：世尊臨入涅槃，文殊請再轉法輪。世尊云：文殊！吾四十九年住世，未甞談一字。今請吾再轉法輪，是吾曾轉法輪耶？師云：文殊為眾竭力，世尊滿口含霜。雖然如是，千言萬語無人會，又逐流鶯過短墻。三月

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings. Baozhi is the named speaker preserved in the first record. His preceding saying has people spending the whole day handling incense and fire while failing to know that the body is itself the place of practice. He then puts his body and all the many kinds of things under the same claim of emptiness. The surrounding verses continue to join form and emptiness while warning against mistaking appearances for something solid. The pair relocates the inquiry from ritual objects alone to one's own body and what is encountered; it is not a report that the world has physically vanished. The headword is rendered: As my body is empty, so are all things; the myriad kinds are alike

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J24/J24nB138.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunmen Kuangzhen. Yunmen Wenyan explicitly raises Baozhi's pair and then addresses ordinary acts: standing, walking, and taking up the bowl to eat. If body and its constituents cannot be grasped, he asks, where do mountains and earth come from, what is called rice, and where is even one grain? The headword remains Baozhi's quoted saying; the questions are Yunmen's current response. They bring the large claim into the listener's own bodily activity and meal, rather than leaving it as an easy statement that all things are empty. The headword is rendered: As my body is empty, so are all things; the myriad kinds are alike

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Tian'an Sheng says the pair directly at an evening gathering, then asks where the monk who died yesterday has gone. His answer is that after ashes have flown and smoke is exhausted, the bell is again heard in the clear night. The shared emptiness claim is thus put to a concrete question about this death and followed by an ordinary present sound. The record supplies no named afterlife destination or assertion that the bell is literally the deceased monk. The headword is rendered: As my body is empty, so are all things; the myriad kinds are alike

Senses.Explanation: Fine spring rain is a soft comparison whose force changes with the turn that carries it. Linji Yixuan applies it to claims that conduct, reason, and guarding the three acts lead to buddhahood; he calls those speakers fox spirits who bind people. Yaofeng Qian gives the same image immediately after denying an auspicious relic story. The phrase does not praise gentle instruction by itself: Linji uses its softness inside a rebuke, while Yaofeng uses it as a terse cap.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB240.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tiebiji of Qingzhong. Qingzhong Tiebi Huiji owns the retained deployment, pairing the doubled grant with a doubled (元來) and sealing the sermon with a shout.

Senses.Explanation: The doubled seal: what the other side just said or showed is granted outright, and the second grant closes the case. Guishan Lingyou crosses his two hands and, when Yangshan answers with a woman's bow, seals it on the spot in his own record; Baizhang Huaihai, in the ancient worthies' record, grants Huangbo's reading of Mazu and straight away warns that view matching the teacher earns only half his virtue; Yangshan Huiji, inside Hongzhi Zhengjue's verse file, seals the monk who takes the future-buddha stance and tells him to guard it well; and the Yi'an master spreads one seal across past, future, and present in answer to the thousand-flower question. Xutang Zhiyu closes the story of meeting his old friend after a dozen years with the bare doubled grant and nothing more; Dahui Zonggao runs his roll-call — the officials, the assembly, himself — and drops the seal before leaving the seat; Jiqi Hongchu, asked whether a guide of the way is really thus, answers with the doubled grant alone; and Qingzhong Tiebi Huiji seals his own sermon on saying-thus and acting-thus, laughs, and shouts.

Senses.Explanation: An ox without horns is Luoshans deliberately impossible answer to a question about sharing life without sharing death. The original reply survives in a useful lamp. Yuanwu and Dahui each raise the exchange in independent current works and interpret its place in Chan encounter; Tiemei and Baiyu deploy the image in other settings. The line disrupts ordinary animal categories to test how the question is heard. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. Baichi Xingyuan owns the retained deployment: verses the mud-pan version of the exchange — the face twisted round and former feeling severed, leaving that one nowhere to hide.

Senses.Explanation: The hinge of a stock exchange: the sentence leans on the tree like a vine, and the question always follows — when the tree falls and the vine withers, where does the sentence go? The answers refuse to fall with it: loud laughter, a slap on the sound, cassia cut from the moon. The Song hinge: Yuanwu Keqin opens a hall address with it — with-sentence and without-sentence overstep lineage and rule, like a vine leaning on a tree, a silver mountain and an iron wall; when the tree falls and the vine withers, how many lose their nostrils, and even those who gather it back up are already a thousand, ten thousand miles out; Dahui Zonggao sets it and prices it — the green-eyed barbarian does not know where it falls; where does it fall? He snaps up the staff, calls the assembly to look, it is coming straight down, eyes sharp, and throws the staff down; Wansong Xingxiu raises the case whole in his comment record — Shushan crosses four thousand li with his cloth roll to ask it, Guishan laughs loudly, and when Shushan protests being toyed with, Guishan calls his attendant to fetch cash. Later answers to the fall: Hanyue Fazang answers the ask with wind and moon year after year while the human heart changes, and the monk bows to the ground — now one knows propriety; Yushan Shangsi takes the ask through the pair, calls the vine-tree the model of old and new, and rules the tree-fall answer one that turns along the speaker's vein, no workman; Yulin Tongxiu at late assembly answers that it is drawn well and painted fine, and at the tree-fall question strikes along with the very sound; the monk before Tian'an Sheng raises the old story of Shushan's ask and Guishan's laugh, and the master answers that the laugh could not be held back; Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the other wing — Shishuang taking leave of Guishan, asked his understanding of the couplet and giving no answer — rules it true, and follows him on to Daowu; Feiyin Tongrong cites Guishan's own version, the mangy horse tied to a withered stump blocking the road the whole year, and at the tree-fall bids one cut the cassia in the moon so the clear light will only be more; Baichi Xingyuan verses the mud-pan version — the face twisted round and former feeling severed, leaving that one nowhere to hide.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛道垂成，十劫觀樹。如虎之缺，如馬之馵。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings. The tiger's nick and the horse's white-marked left hind foot are paired marks that later readers interpret differently. In the Dongshan section, the Jewel-Mirror verse places them immediately after the Buddha-way nearing completion and ten aeons spent contemplating a tree. The difficult images belong to that warning about attainment, not to a zoological account; the short retained span does not by itself settle the precise application of each mark. Later teaching turns retain their difficulty instead of supplying one uncontested meaning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 末後又道：『我未曾譚著一字。』盂上座也是抴尾靈龜，無事生事。不見道：『如虎之缺，如馬之馵。』」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB189.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Sanyi Yu. Sanyi Mingyu quotes the pair after challenging the Buddha's final claim that he had never spoken a word. Sanyi includes himself as a turtle dragging its tail, making trouble where none was needed, then invokes the tiger and horse. The inherited marks serve a self-implicating check on speech about speech: even the comment risks leaving another trace. The exact pair is a quotation from the older verse, while Sanyi is the present critic rather than a new author of it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 頌曰：海潮聲裡依稀，沙界堆頭流注。既非頷下神珠，何故兩手分付？撥波求水事應難，寥寥萬古真奇遇。全身擔負得來，應知利害去處。咄！如虎之缺，如馬之馵。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB286.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yingningjing. Yingning Zhijing voices the pair at the end of his own verse on a patriarchal encounter. He asks why something that is not the spirit pearl under the dragon's jaw is nevertheless handed over with both hands, says seeking water by pushing aside waves is difficult, and urges someone bearing the whole matter to know where benefit and danger lie. After a shout come the tiger and horse. The marks cap this warning about handling and transmission; the stanza does not explicitly identify a single fault to be assigned to either animal or interlocutor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 太宰問：「寶鏡三昧中所云：『如虎之缺，如馬之馵。』此二句若以道理註解，或即應下文。以有下劣，故拖泥帶水，以示敗闕。因為救人，不嫌自敗，捨位就功，故云寶几珍御。如此解，不知合否？望師以道理判示，不敢當上上機也。」師曰：「寶鏡謂佛道垂成云者，正恐大通智勝，自滯空劫，猶十劫觀樹，而佛法不得現前也。故有三墮之設，欲其不觸虎頭之缺，與犯馬足之馵，而迥超於功位耳。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB311.xml). Complete Record of Chan Master Juelangsheng of Tianjie. A lay dignitary asks Juelang Daosheng whether the two lines can be explained as showing one's own shortcoming to rescue others, leaving rank to undertake effective work. Juelang instead stresses the preceding 'Buddha-way nearing completion': he fears the figure of Great Penetrating Wisdom remaining stuck in an empty aeon, contemplating a tree while the teaching does not become present. He invokes the three falls as a way to avoid touching the tiger's nick or transgressing the horse's marking and to move beyond merit and position. Dongshan owns the cited words; the dignitary's proposed gloss and Juelang's corrective interpretation must remain distinct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如虎之缺，如馬之馵。虎一名李耳，虎食畜不至耳，又每食人耳，則耳必一缺，此以例不敢犯諱也。馵者，馬後左脚間有白色也，此以例語忌十成也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian. Yongjue Yuanxian glosses the old verse with specific traditional explanations. He connects the tiger's missing ear with its alternative name Li'er and an avoidance taboo, and identifies the horse's marking as white on its left hind leg, applying it to the caution against language claiming complete perfection. These are Yongjue's explanations of the images, not independent natural-history findings. His gloss grounds the translation of the bodily marks while showing how the pair can warn against crossing a verbal limit.

Senses.PreferredTarget: like a tiger fitted with horns
AlternateTargets: like a tiger bearing horns
Senses.Note: The comparison adds horns to a tiger. Tianyin Yuanxiu pairs it with a bird riding its wings, while Zhenjing Kewen and Yuanwu Keqin use it for something already vividly active or formidable. One lamp recension preserves Luoshan Daoxian's paired horned-tiger and hornless-ox answers; its question order differs from Yuanwu's stronger recorded version.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record by Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo: within the Luoshan case raised by Yuanwu Keqin, Luoshan Daoxian is the quoted original utterer. Senses.Explanation: Literally, 如虎戴角 is 'like a tiger fitted with horns': horns are added to an animal already equipped with teeth, claws, and force. Tianyin Yuanxiu makes that addition explicit by pairing the horned tiger with a bird riding its wings. Zhenjing Kewen uses the comparison after describing the great matter as wholly appearing, alive, colliding, and gnashing. Yuanwu Keqin says that understanding Xuedou Chongxian's verse would be like a tiger fitted with horns; elsewhere he calls Zun the patch-robed monk a horned tiger with awe-inspiring force. The Luoshan Daoxian exchange pairs the horned tiger with a hornless ox. Its surviving recensions reverse which of the two birth-and-death questions receives which answer, so the article preserves the disagreement instead of assigning the image a single answer-specific doctrine.

Senses.Explanation: Like an insect boring through wood and accidentally forming writing: a figure for an apparent pattern produced without deliberate mastery. Senses.Explanation: The pair compares a response to a struck bell and a valley receiving sound. Yuanwu Keqin compares Dongshan Shouchu's answer to a bell answering when struck and a valley receiving a sound. Yuanwu immediately says that large and small are answered according to what arrives and that Dongshan did not respond lightly.

Senses.Explanation: The records complete the comparison as “like a bell on its stand: when struck, it sounds,” pairing it with a mirror that reflects whatever comes before it. Senses.Explanation: An impossible-birth comparison, 'as if a pillar were pregnant,' used to press what is present before a distinction or how a fixed thing could give birth. In a case raised in Hengchuan Rugong's record, Lingyun Zhiqin answers Changsheng's question about the time before division with the pillar carrying a fetus. Yingning Zhijing later asks Tianzhu whether that fetus is male or female; Tianzhu pinches his knee and leaves. Baiyu Jingsi sets the pregnant pillar beside a laughing lantern at a Buddha-birthday address and asks what the pair makes clear. Shiyu Mingfang pairs it with a bull bearing a calf when he challenges the assembly to account for an auspicious birth. Tianran Hanshi includes it among images that cannot be settled by merely calling them real or unreal.

AlternateTargets: Like wind over water, patterns arise naturally
Senses.Note: Read each instance with its nearby action. It can praise natural conduct, freedom within retreat discipline, timely recognition, or unforced verse making; the simile alone does not settle which.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Neishaozhong, Neishao Zhizhong speaks in his own hall sermon, not as a narrator of an older case. He begins with ordinary responses: warming oneself by a fire, feeling cold wind, eating when hungry, and sleeping when tired. A pearl rolls on its plate without being pushed; wind makes ripples on water of itself. The quoted image names that unforced working. Neishao immediately warns that the matter cannot be reached by sense perception or calculating thought, then raises a hypothetical shout from Gaofeng, gives a shout himself, and asks the assembly why it is dozing. The shout and challenge are his continuation of the same sermon, not part of the ripple simile.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huiyue Xu, Huiyue gives a short address at the opening of the summer retreat. He first rejects a merely clever reading of the retreat saying about killing and protecting life, then sets three concrete requirements for his monks: live harmoniously, keep the settled routine in all postures, and be free and open rather than work in a ghost cave. Once those duties are in place, he says the monkey may roam up and down the trees; he then asks why and answers with wind naturally making ripples on water. Here the line explains freedom arising in disciplined practice. He next cites Wuzu and comments on that older summer-retreat address; Wuzu is a later quoted speaker, not the voice of Huiyue’s ripple line.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xixinshui of Xiangyan, Xixin Zhaoshui draws a sign in the air with his staff during a hall address. He says the news it conveys can be missed in a blink, and that an alert monk should grasp it before the gesture is even made. Only then does he say that one may move freely, like wind making ripples on water of itself. Xixin looks around and asks whether anyone is such a person. A monk steps forward, but Xixin says the sword departed long ago while the monk is still marking the boat to find it; when the monk hesitates, Xixin strikes him. The natural ripple image is part of Xixin’s challenge to timely recognition, not a promise that the monk’s late answer succeeds.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Expanded Record of Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan, Xiatang directly instructs his brothers about practice and verse making. He urges them to work with a live saying rather than cling to dead wording, and says beginners may try composing verses as an exercise in rubbing down their habits of thought. But after the central matter is clearly understood, they need not deliberately make verses: they form naturally, as wind makes ripples on water. He goes on to show how earlier masters versified old cases; those cited verses are examples in his instruction, not the source of this line. The image concerns unforced expression after understanding, not a ban on beginners’ practice.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Neishaozhong, Neishao Zhizhong speaks in his own hall sermon, not as a narrator of an older case. He begins with ordinary responses: warming oneself by a fire, feeling cold wind, eating when hungry, and sleeping when tired. A pearl rolls on its plate without being pushed; wind makes ripples on water of itself. The quoted image names that unforced working. Neishao immediately warns that the matter cannot be reached by sense perception or calculating thought, then raises a hypothetical shout from Gaofeng, gives a shout himself, and asks the assembly why it is dozing. The shout and challenge are his continuation of the same sermon, not part of the ripple simile.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huiyue Xu, Huiyue gives a short address at the opening of the summer retreat. He first rejects a merely clever reading of the retreat saying about killing and protecting life, then sets three concrete requirements for his monks: live harmoniously, keep the settled routine in all postures, and be free and open rather than work in a ghost cave. Once those duties are in place, he says the monkey may roam up and down the trees; he then asks why and answers with wind naturally making ripples on water. Here the line explains freedom arising in disciplined practice. He next cites Wuzu and comments on that older summer-retreat address; Wuzu is a later quoted speaker, not the voice of Huiyue’s ripple line.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xixinshui of Xiangyan, Xixin Zhaoshui draws a sign in the air with his staff during a hall address. He says the news it conveys can be missed in a blink, and that an alert monk should grasp it before the gesture is even made. Only then does he say that one may move freely, like wind making ripples on water of itself. Xixin looks around and asks whether anyone is such a person. A monk steps forward, but Xixin says the sword departed long ago while the monk is still marking the boat to find it; when the monk hesitates, Xixin strikes him. The natural ripple image is part of Xixin’s challenge to timely recognition, not a promise that the monk’s late answer succeeds.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: In Expanded Record of Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan, Xiatang directly instructs his brothers about practice and verse making. He urges them to work with a live saying rather than cling to dead wording, and says beginners may try composing verses as an exercise in rubbing down their habits of thought. But after the central matter is clearly understood, they need not deliberately make verses: they form naturally, as wind makes ripples on water. He goes on to show how earlier masters versified old cases; those cited verses are examples in his instruction, not the source of this line. The image concerns unforced expression after understanding, not a ban on beginners’ practice.

Senses.Explanation: The image compares wind raising ripples on water with response or expression that arises without strain. Neishao places it among ordinary acts before a shout that jolts his assembly; Huiyue uses it after three duties for the summer retreat; Xixin sets it against a monk who responds too late to his staff sign; Xiatang applies it to verses that emerge after the central matter is understood. These are four current speakers in four distinct records, each with a different local teaching point.

Fachang Yiyu, pressed at the end of a question round — the dharma all on his staff's tip, the blind man groping under the noon sun — dismisses the questioner's polite retreat with the verdict: disorderly Chan-wanderers, thick as hemp and millet. Xuedou Chongxian, appraising the two elders of the Wuzhou-ridge meeting in the Classified Anthology — one only releases, one only holds — waits a long beat, then rules: board-carrying Chan-wanderers, thick as hemp and millet. And Zhantang Wenzhun, finding his young student reading the Diamond Sutra and testing him on the dharma's evenness against Yunju's height and Baofeng's lowness, drops the same brand on the answer and walks out — the student, standing behind, secretly delighted that an eyed teacher knows he is already on the right road. Gulin Qingmao, after a visiting monk performs his one-word-severs-a-thousand-rivers flourish without a word of his own, brands the shape: disorderly Chan-wanderers, thick as hemp and millet. Liangting Jingting, defending sutra study against the throw-away-everything crowd, counts them off — cooked-up elders, thick as hemp and millet, who read no sutras, practice no deportment, call it the shortcut, and set up shop as village gate-masters with a few memorized set pieces. So why could none of them handle it? And Hanyue Fazang, drumming on an awning of void with sun and moon for drumsticks to summon five hundred wooden arhats from Deng Mountain to haul firewood and steam millet on Rice-Hoard Peak, inverts the measure — the three-times buddhas themselves thick as hemp and millet, applauding in empty space, with only Samantabhadra's eldest son riding the reclining-elephant peak as witness.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue. Dahui says those discussing two old cases are as numerous as hemp and millet before criticizing wrong readings.

Senses.Explanation: The comparison means an uncountable multitude. Its force depends on what the local sentence counts: deadened Chan students, accomplished monks, or generations of eminent teachers. Ling Xingpo dismisses ‘dead Chan fellows’ as numerous as hemp and millet; a preface to Wuhuan's record says people who settled the great matter were so numerous; the Miyin monastery account applies it to eminent figures flourishing over centuries. Zishui uses it for worldly clever people in his own instruction; Dahui uses it for the many monks who discuss two old cases, before correcting mistaken readings. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.

Senses.Explanation: To distinguish black from white is to discriminate clearly between what an encounter, saying, or lineage claim does and does not amount to. Masters demand this hair's-breadth discrimination and condemn indiscriminate handling. Baoning says one must distinguish black from white, since a hair's breadth weighs more than mountains. Yuanwu says the Four Classifications distinguish black from white. Poshan condemns following others without distinguishing black from white. Muchen calls for someone able to distinguish black from white and know the weight. Feiyin condemns people who do not know black from white yet speak recklessly.
